# The `sf` object {#sec-m2-sf} `sf` (*simple features*) is the standard for vector data in R. The central idea is simple and solves half of geoprocessing problems: **an `sf` object is a `data.frame` with a geometry column**. Everything you learned in module 1 (`filter`, `mutate`, `summarise`, `join`) still applies, and the geometry follows along through the operations. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(sf) library(dplyr) library(ggplot2) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sf::sf_extSoftVersion() #> GEOS GDAL proj.4 GDAL_with_GEOS USE_PROJ_H #> "3.14.1" "3.12.1" "9.7.1" "true" "true" #> PROJ #> "9.7.1" ``` ::: These are the libraries that do the heavy lifting: GDAL (reading/writing formats), PROJ (projections) and GEOS (geometric operations). They are the same ones QGIS uses underneath. R is not a "weaker" alternative: it is the same machine with a different interface. ## Building geometries by hand To understand the structure, it is worth building each type of geometry once. We will use real ports as the example. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # point porto <- sf::st_point(c(-48.5, -25.5)) class(porto) #> [1] "XY" "POINT" "sfg" # from a table of coordinates: the most common case day to day. # instead of typing the coordinates by hand, we read a real file with # the location of port facilities from ANTAQ's register portos_tab <- readr::read_csv("dados/portos_antaq.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) portos_tab ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} portos <- sf::st_as_sf(portos_tab, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326) portos ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Read carefully the header `sf` prints: number of features, geometry type, dimension, `bbox` (bounding box) and the **CRS**. It is the first thing to check in any spatial dataset. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Before the first map: choose a basemap that does not need an API key Some options in `mapview`'s default list (such as those from Stadia Maps) now require registration and an API key. To avoid this, set once, at the start of the session, a list of free basemaps with no registration: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mapview::mapviewOptions(basemaps = c("OpenStreetMap", "Esri.WorldGrayCanvas", "Esri.WorldImagery")) ``` ::: This option applies to every `mapview()` in the session, including those in this chapter. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mapview::mapview(portos) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: `mapview()` is the quickest way to check whether spatial data are where they should be: an interactive map, with zoom and attribute popups, from any `sf` object. We come back to it in every chapter of this module, whenever there is a spatial result to check. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Large datasets make `mapview()` slow With many features (a whole set of municipal boundaries, a road network), the default `mapview()` can freeze the browser. The `leafgl` package renders the same thing with WebGL, much faster. Just install `leafgl` and switch the drawing platform once, at the start of the session: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} install.packages("leafgl") mapview::mapviewOptions(platform = "leafgl") ``` ::: After that, every `mapview::mapview(objeto_sf)` in the session uses `leafgl` automatically. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} class(portos) #> [1] "sf" "tbl_df" "tbl" "data.frame" sf::st_geometry_type(portos, by_geometry = FALSE) #> [1] POINT #> 18 Levels: GEOMETRY POINT LINESTRING POLYGON MULTIPOINT ... TRIANGLE sf::st_bbox(portos) #> xmin ymin xmax ymax #> -48.6486 -26.9077 -38.8000 -3.5500 sf::st_crs(portos)$input #> [1] "EPSG:4326" ``` ::: `st_as_sf()` with `coords =` is probably the function you will use most: it turns any spreadsheet with latitude and longitude into spatial data. ::: {.callout-warning} ## The order is longitude, latitude `coords = c("lon", "lat")`: **x first**. Reversed, your points land in the Indian Ocean or in Antarctica. When the map comes out empty or with absurd points, this is the first suspect. ::: ### Lines and polygons ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # line: a sequence of points trecho <- sf::st_linestring(rbind( c(-48.51, -25.50), c(-48.80, -25.42), c(-49.27, -25.43) )) # polygon: closed ring (first point = last point) quadra <- sf::st_polygon(list(rbind( c(-48.6, -25.6), c(-48.4, -25.6), c(-48.4, -25.4), c(-48.6, -25.4), c(-48.6, -25.6) ))) sf::st_sfc(trecho, quadra, crs = 4326) |> sf::st_geometry_type() #> [1] LINESTRING POLYGON #> 18 Levels: GEOMETRY POINT LINESTRING POLYGON MULTIPOINT ... TRIANGLE sf::st_length(sf::st_sfc(trecho, crs = 4326)) #> 77656.72 [m] sf::st_area(sf::st_sfc(quadra, crs = 4326)) #> 446395208 [m^2] ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mapview::mapview(sf::st_sfc(trecho, crs = 4326), color = "#1a5b8a") + mapview::mapview(sf::st_sfc(quadra, crs = 4326), col.regions = "#e07b39") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Notice that `st_length()` and `st_area()` return the result **with units** (metres, square metres). `sf` uses the `units` package. This prevents the classic mistake of reporting area in decimal degrees: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} area <- sf::st_area(sf::st_sfc(quadra, crs = 4326)) units::set_units(area, km^2) #> 446.3952 [km^2] as.numeric(units::set_units(area, km^2)) # to use in a calculation or chart #> [1] 446.3952 ``` ::: ### Geometry types | Type | What it is | Example in our context | |:--|:--|:--| | `POINT` | one point | port facility, counting station, bus stop | | `MULTIPOINT` | several points in one feature | set of entrances to a terminal | | `LINESTRING` | one line | highway segment, railway line | | `MULTILINESTRING` | several lines in one feature | a whole highway, with discontinuous segments | | `POLYGON` | one area | municipality, census tract, catchment area | | `MULTIPOLYGON` | several areas in one feature | municipality with islands, state with enclaves | | `GEOMETRYCOLLECTION` | a mix of types | result of some intersections | In practice, IBGE boundaries come as `MULTIPOLYGON` and road networks as `MULTILINESTRING`, because a feature can be physically discontinuous. When a function requires a specific type, convert: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sf::st_cast(x, "POLYGON") # splits each part into a row of the table sf::st_cast(x, "MULTIPOLYGON") # groups them sf::st_collection_extract(x, "POLYGON") # discards what is not a polygon ``` ::: ## Reading files `st_read()` reads practically any vector format. GDAL decides based on what it recognises in the extension. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sf::st_read("dados/brutos/snv/SNV_202601A.shp") # Shapefile sf::st_read("dados/brutos/base.gpkg", layer = "rodovias") # GeoPackage (several layers) sf::st_read("dados/brutos/limites.geojson") sf::st_read("dados/brutos/base.sqlite", layer = "portos") # SQLite/Spatialite sf::st_layers("dados/brutos/base.gpkg") # which layers exist in the file ``` ::: Arguments that solve the most frequent problems: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sf::st_read("arquivo.shp", quiet = TRUE) # without the reading message sf::st_read("arquivo.shp", options = "ENCODING=LATIN1") # accents in an old shapefile sf::st_read("arquivo.shp", query = "SELECT * FROM arquivo WHERE sg_uf = 'PR'") # filters while reading sf::st_read("arquivo.gpkg", wkt_filter = sf::st_as_text(sf::st_geometry(area))) # spatial crop ``` ::: The last two matter with large datasets: instead of loading 500 MB of national boundaries only to filter one state afterwards, the filter goes along with the reading. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Shapefile or GeoPackage? The Shapefile (`.shp`) is the most widespread format, but it has real limitations: it is 4 to 6 files that must travel together, column names limited to 10 characters, and problems with accents. The **GeoPackage** (`.gpkg`) is a single file, without these limits, with several layers inside. For working files and results, use `.gpkg`; keep `.shp` only when the recipient requires it. ::: ## Writing ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dir.create("resultados", showWarnings = FALSE) sf::st_write(portos, "resultados/portos.gpkg", delete_dsn = TRUE) # overwrites the file sf::st_write(portos, "resultados/portos.shp") sf::st_write(portos, "resultados/portos.geojson") # several layers in the same GeoPackage sf::st_write(portos, "resultados/analise.gpkg", layer = "portos") sf::st_write(trechos, "resultados/analise.gpkg", layer = "trechos", append = TRUE) # table without geometry, for Excel portos |> sf::st_drop_geometry() |> writexl::write_xlsx("resultados/portos.xlsx") # coordinates as columns portos |> dplyr::mutate(lon = sf::st_coordinates(geometry)[, 1], lat = sf::st_coordinates(geometry)[, 2]) |> sf::st_drop_geometry() |> readr::write_csv("resultados/portos.csv") ``` ::: `st_drop_geometry()` is the shortcut back to an ordinary `data.frame`. It is useful when the geometry has done its job and you just want the table. ## `dplyr` verbs on `sf` objects ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} portos |> dplyr::filter(uf %in% c("PR", "SC")) |> dplyr::mutate(regiao = "Sul") |> dplyr::select(nome, uf, regiao) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: The geometry is "sticky": it survives `filter`, `mutate`, `select` and `arrange` without you asking. Two exceptions worth knowing. Note that, on `sf` objects, grouping is done with `group_by()`, not with module 1's `.by` argument, which the `sf` method does not implement: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # summarise aggregates the geometries (union) within each group portos |> dplyr::group_by(uf) |> dplyr::summarise(n = dplyr::n()) |> sf::st_geometry_type() #> [1] POINT POINT POINT POINT #> 18 Levels: GEOMETRY POINT LINESTRING POLYGON MULTIPOINT ... TRIANGLE ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # to aggregate ONLY the attributes, remove the geometry first portos |> sf::st_drop_geometry() |> dplyr::count(uf) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ## Quick inspection of a new spatial dataset The routine worth running whenever you open an unknown file. To keep it concrete, we apply it straight to the `portos` object we already have: in your case, start by replacing the first line with `x <- sf::st_read("arquivo.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- portos nrow(x) # how many features #> [1] 4 sf::st_geometry_type(x, by_geometry = FALSE) # what type of geometry #> [1] POINT #> 18 Levels: GEOMETRY POINT LINESTRING POLYGON MULTIPOINT ... TRIANGLE sf::st_crs(x)$input # which coordinate system #> [1] "EPSG:4326" sf::st_bbox(x) # where it is (as expected?) #> xmin ymin xmax ymax #> -48.6486 -26.9077 -38.8000 -3.5500 names(x) # which attributes #> [1] "nome" "uf" "geometry" all(sf::st_is_valid(x)) # is the geometry valid? #> [1] TRUE mapview::mapview(x) # does the drawing make sense? ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: `st_is_valid()` deserves attention: invalid geometries (self-intersections, reversed rings) are common in old shapefiles and make later operations fail with obscure messages. The fix is one line: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- sf::st_make_valid(x) ``` :::
